TIP 1: Inflated speaker fees flowing to interventional cardiologists at major heart center
CHANNEL: encrypted email
RECEIVED: 28 April 2026

I am writing about Lattimer Medical, a Minneapolis-based medical device manufacturer that markets a portfolio of drug-eluting coronary stents. I work in Lattimer's compliance organization as an associate director with primary responsibility for HCP (healthcare professional) payments review. I have been at Lattimer since 2022.

The issue I am reporting is a pattern of speaker bureau and consulting payments to a defined group of interventional cardiologists at one institution that, in my professional judgment, do not correspond to actual speaker or consulting work and instead function as compensation for institutional purchasing preference.

The institution is Mercer Heart Institute, an academic cardiac center affiliated with a large midwestern medical school. Mercer's cath lab performs approximately 4,200 percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) procedures annually and is among the top fifty PCI volume centers in the country. Lattimer's stent portfolio holds approximately 78 percent of Mercer's stent volume — well above our 31 percent national share.

Across calendar years 2023 through 2025, Lattimer paid eleven physicians at Mercer a combined $4.7 million in HCP payments — speaker fees, consulting fees, and research grants. The five highest-paid physicians received between $312,000 and $548,000 each in 2025 alone. All eleven are interventional cardiologists with personal procedure volume that drives stent selection in their respective cath labs.

What concerns me on review is what these payments correspond to.

First, the speaker fees: my audit of speaker bureau records for 2024 identified that of the 187 paid "speaking events" attributed to the Mercer-affiliated speakers, 143 were closed-list dinners at high-end restaurants in the Mercer metro area, with attendance lists that consisted primarily of other Mercer interventional cardiologists. The "training content" delivered at these events, where it was documented at all, is described in vague clinical-update language. There are no slide decks retained for 91 of the 143.

Second, the consulting fees: Mercer's Dr. R. Vehring is paid $96,000 per quarter on a "scientific advisor" agreement. Across 2024 and 2025 I can find approximately fourteen hours of documented Vehring consulting deliverables — a few email replies on protocol design and one half-day advisory board appearance.

Third, the research grants: three "investigator-initiated" research grants to Mercer-led studies of Lattimer products in 2023-2024, totaling $1.8 million, do not have corresponding study enrollment records that match the budget burn. Two of the three studies have not enrolled a single subject as of my last review.

I have raised these patterns with my supervisor and with our Chief Compliance Officer. The response in both cases has been that the payments are within "fair market value" benchmarks and that audit findings should focus on individual compliance gaps rather than aggregate purchasing pattern correlation.

I have retained the relevant payment records, the speaker bureau attendance and content logs, the consulting agreement deliverables, and the IIS budget-versus-enrollment data.

TIP 2: Lost competitive bid at major academic heart center despite superior data
CHANNEL: secure drop
RECEIVED: 03 May 2026

I am a senior account executive for Vorian Medical, a publicly traded medical device manufacturer that competes in the coronary stent market. I have been with Vorian since 2018. I cover a midwestern territory that includes Mercer Heart Institute, an academic cardiac center I have called on without successfully winning the account for over five years.

I am submitting this because what I have observed at Mercer over the past three years has crossed, in my view, from a competitive disadvantage we should be able to overcome with data and price into something that I believe is corruptly determined. I want to be clear that I am writing this as someone with an obvious commercial motive, but the underlying facts are documented and I am willing to share them.

In April 2024 Mercer ran its standard biennial value-analysis review for its drug-eluting stent contract. Vorian submitted a competitive proposal. Our offering had three documented advantages over Lattimer Medical's incumbent product:

- Pricing: 22 percent lower per-unit than Lattimer's then-current contracted price, with a no-cost on-shelf consignment program that further reduced Mercer's working-capital requirement.
- Outcomes: published 5-year MACE rates from a randomized trial of approximately 8,400 patients showed Vorian's product non-inferior at 12 months and superior at 60 months on the composite endpoint, a result Lattimer has no comparable head-to-head data to refute.
- Service: two regional clinical specialists with over 20 years of cath lab experience, available on-site for procedural support.

Mercer's value-analysis committee reviewed the proposal in May 2024. The committee's recommendation, which I obtained through a contact who later left Mercer for an unrelated reason, was to "transition a portion of the stent volume to Vorian on a phased basis subject to outcomes monitoring."

Mercer's CFO and Chair of Cardiology overrode the value-analysis recommendation. The contract was renewed with Lattimer at the existing pricing tier. The reason given to me by Mercer's purchasing director, on a 12 June 2024 phone call I documented in my CRM, was: "your data doesn't matter, we have a clinical relationship with Lattimer that this institution is not going to walk away from over a price difference." Those are the words on my CRM contact note.

In the following 18 months I have continued to call on Mercer interventionalists. I have personally watched Lattimer reps deliver lunch trays to the cath lab break room on the same days that Mercer attendings are returning from "speaking engagements" Lattimer paid them for. The pattern is observable and not hidden.

I am not in a position to allege fraud — I do not have access to Lattimer's payment records or to Mercer's internal procurement deliberations. What I can say is that the customary considerations of price, outcomes data, and service did not control this decision, and that the publicly disclosable Open Payments data shows Lattimer paying eleven Mercer interventionalists very large amounts of money during the same period.

I will identify myself to a reporter or investigator under conditions that protect my employment. I have my CRM notes, the Vorian proposal, the Open Payments lookups I ran, and a contemporaneous email from my regional manager acknowledging the loss. Vorian leadership is aware I am pursuing this externally and has not asked me to stand down, but they also have not joined the disclosure.

TIP 3: Stent selection pressure during cardiology fellowship at academic heart center
CHANNEL: intake form
RECEIVED: 05 May 2026

I am a third-year interventional cardiology fellow at Mercer Heart Institute, where I have trained since 2023. I am submitting this anonymously because the cardiology training community in this country is small enough that I would be identifiable to anyone who knows the program, and any retaliation would end my career before it has begun.

I am writing about what I have observed during my training regarding stent selection in the cath lab and the relationship between my attending physicians and Lattimer Medical, the company whose stents are used in approximately three quarters of our cases.

The first thing I noticed when I started fellowship was that we use Lattimer stents almost exclusively. In the device-selection portion of our case-planning conferences, alternative manufacturers' products are mentioned occasionally but rarely chosen. When I asked one of my attendings — Dr. R. Vehring, in my first month on the rotation — why we chose Lattimer for a particular complex bifurcation case where I had read about a competitor's product showing better data, Dr. Vehring told me: "we use Lattimer here, you'll learn the platform and you'll be good at it." He did not engage with the comparative data point.

In the cath lab break room there is a pinboard where the attendings post the Open Payments disclosure forms they are required to make available. I have read these forms. Five of the seven attendings I have rotated under in my fellowship have annual Lattimer payments above $250,000 in the most recent disclosure period. One — I will not name them — has a 2024 disclosed payment total of more than half a million dollars.

The "speaker training" sessions that the fellowship is sometimes invited to as observers are dinners at restaurants downtown. The clinical content portion of these sessions is short. When clinical content is delivered, it is usually a Lattimer product slide deck presented by a Lattimer field educator, with one of our attendings hosting and moderating but not actually presenting original work. I have attended four such dinners during my training to date.

I want to be careful about what I am alleging and what I am not. I cannot tell you that any individual case in my training was managed worse because a Lattimer product was used. The Lattimer products are FDA-approved and clinically appropriate for many of our cases. What I can say is that the selection of device in our cath lab is not driven by the kind of evidence-based, case-specific reasoning I was taught to expect during fellowship. The pattern of compensation to my attendings is large enough that I have come to believe it is the actual operating consideration.

I do not have documents to provide beyond what I have personally observed. I cannot share patient records and would not. I am willing to speak with a reporter or investigator if I can do so under conditions that do not identify me to my program. I am also willing, if necessary, to redirect any inquiry to one of my co-fellows who has expressed similar concerns.
